d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of anodize.
to coat the surface of a metal electrolytically with an oxide, either as protection or decoration

anodize.e: English anode Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English anodize From anode + -ize.

d.g: To smear or rub over with oil or an unctuous substance; also, to spread over, as oil.
d.x: He anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay.

d.g: To apply oil to or to pour oil upon, etc., as a sacred rite, especially for consecration.
d.x: Then shalt thou take the anointing oil, and pour it upon his [Aaron's] head and anoint him.

d.g: To choose or nominate somebody for a leading or otherwise important position, especially formally or officially, or as an intended successor.
To mark somebody as an official ruler, especially a king or queen, as a part of a religious ceremony.

anoint.e: From Middle English enointen, anointen, borrowed from Old French enoint, past participle of enoindre (“to anoint”). Doublet of inunct.

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of antagonize.
To work against; to oppose (especially to incite a reaction).
d.x: The other children constantly antagonized Joe to the point of tears.

antagonize.e: From Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai), from ἀντι- (anti-) + ἀγωνίζομαι (agōnízomai). By surface analysis, ant- + agon + -ize.

d.g: To go before; to precede.
To predate or antedate.
To occur before an event or time; to exist further back in time.
d.x: Actually, mathematical models of multi-sector growth models antedate the Harrod-Domar and Solow-Swan aggregate models.

d.g: To assign a date to a document or action earlier than the actual date.
d.x: Tomorrow when you leav’st, what wilt thou say? / Wilt thou then antedate some new-made vow?

d.g: To find earlier citational evidence for a term.
Prior date; a date antecedent to another which is the actual date.

antedate.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₂énts Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti Proto-Italic *anti Classical Latin ante Classical Latin ante-lbor. English ante- English date English antedate From ante- + date.

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of anthologize.
To gather a collection of written works for publication.
To include a written work in a published collection of works.

anthologize.e: English anthology Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English anthologize From anthology + -ize.

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of anthropomorphize.
d.x: Certainly we seem to readily anthropomorphise inanimate objects […]

d.g: To endow with human qualities.
To ascribe or attribute human characteristics and behaviors to entities.
d.x: Bonnie Lucas further anthropomorphizes the flower in her watercolors, combining it surreally with the human female figure[…]

d.g: To act before (someone), especially to prevent an action.
d.x: He would probably have died by the hand of the executioner, if indeed the executioner had not been anticipated by the populace.

d.g: To take up or introduce (something) prematurely.
d.x: The advocate plans to anticipate a part of her argument.

d.g: To know of (something) before it happens; to expect.
d.x: to anticipate the pleasures of a visit

d.g: To eagerly wait for (something)
d.x: Little Johnny started to anticipate the arrival of Santa Claus a week before Christmas.

anticipate.e: Borrowed from Latin anticipātus, perfect passive participle of anticipō (“to anticipate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ante- (“before”), + capiō (“to take”, cip- when prefixed) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See capable.

d.g: To cause to become old or obsolete.

antiquate.e: From Latin antiquātus, perfect passive participle of antiquō (“to make old, restore to a pristine state”). Also see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To make antiseptic.
